# Craftar

> Open-source CLI (TypeScript/Node) that treats an AI-coding harness (rules, agents, commands, skills, hooks, MCP servers) as source in a Git repository (the Forge), composes it per team from reusable ingredients, and emits it in the native format of each AI coder (Claude Code, Kiro, AGENTS.md, Cursor, Copilot, Agent Skills, Codex, Antigravity and, as mvp, OpenCode) into every workspace, with a lockfile for drift detection and a per-machine registry of workspaces.

This file is the plain-text companion of the Craftar site, the home page (index.html), the documentation (docs/index.html) and the changelog (changelog/index.html), written for language models and other automated readers. Same content, no layout; diagrams are described in prose (verbatim from the accessible description of each figure) and the two whose topology carries the argument are also given as Mermaid graphs.

## At a glance (the hero)

A build system for AI-coding harnesses. A harness (the rules, agents, commands, skills, hooks and MCP servers that shape coding agents) kept as source in one Git repository, the Forge; Craftar composes it per team, writes each tool's own files and records them in a lockfile.

Below the title, a demo with two menus: the action (Get an update from the Forge, Send an edit to the Forge) and where it runs (In Orca; In the console), and four animated screens, synthetic `acme` data:

- In Orca, get an update: an Orca-style window, the workspace list (acme: acme-portal, acme-api), Source Control, and the craftar for Orca panel docked on the right, drawn by the plugin's own code (build 51f2036) on synthetic data. The panel shows the Forge (`forge`, default branch @ b83f2d6, ../forge, on this machine), craftar sync with "2 coming down from the Forge" (commit 7c41e0a → b83f2d6), the surfaces (agents-md up to date, claude-code and kiro outdated, 1 to update each), the workspace (acme-portal, profile acme-portal, lock forge@7c41e0a), From the Forge (`workflow.md` in `.claude/rules/` and `.kiro/steering/`) and the footer button "Bring 2 from the Forge" (bring: writes and stages · send: dry run first · never a commit). Bring opens "Update 2 files and add them to your commit?" (written and staged: the two files and craftar.lock) with "Update and stage" (never --overwrite-drift · never a commit); then the panel reads in sync, with the last update's written and staged files, and Source Control lists the three staged paths.
- In Orca, send an edit: a line is typed into `.claude/rules/commit-conventions.md`; the panel shows "1 can go up to the Forge" (edited here by hand · kept on every sync), claude-code in drift, Edited here with an orange Send, and "Send 1 to the Forge"; the dry run asks "Send .claude/rules/commit-conventions.md to the Forge?" (outcome variant, becomes rule/commit-conventions--acme-portal, profile acme-portal; craftar would write the variant's two files and recipes/acme-portal-base.yaml; this workspace's next sync unchanged 9; other workspaces on this Forge none; no warnings) with "Write to the Forge" (writes the Forge's working tree · nothing is committed, pushed or opened as a PR); then "Written to the Forge's working tree: nothing was committed", and "Back to the workspace".
- Under the window: craftar (the CLI and this plugin) is built with Orca (https://onorca.dev), which is why the example runs in it. Get the Orca plugin: https://github.com/llima/craftar-orca#install
- In the console, get an update (craftar 1.7.0; the comment line stands for the Forge commit):

```
# the Forge moved: a rule was edited and committed in acme-forge
$ craftar status
craftar status — profile acme · recipes base
  update 2
  update        .claude/rules/project-conventions.md  rule/project-conventions
  update        .kiro/steering/project-conventions.md  rule/project-conventions
$ craftar sync
craftar sync — profile acme · recipes base · targets claude-code, kiro
  wrote 2, removed 0 orphan(s), skipped 0
  + .claude/rules/project-conventions.md
  + .kiro/steering/project-conventions.md
```

- In the console, send an edit (craftar 1.7.0; the comment line stands for the hand edit):

```
# a line was added to .claude/rules/project-conventions.md by hand
$ craftar drift show
drift         .claude/rules/project-conventions.md  rule/project-conventions  forge: same  promote: yes
$ craftar drift promote .claude/rules/project-conventions.md --dry-run
promote .claude/rules/project-conventions.md → rule/project-conventions--acme (variant, profile acme)
  would write ingredients/rules/project-conventions--acme/ingredient.yaml
  would write ingredients/rules/project-conventions--acme/rule.md
  would edit recipes/base.yaml (ingredients)
  dry run — the Forge was not written
$ craftar drift promote .claude/rules/project-conventions.md
promote .claude/rules/project-conventions.md → rule/project-conventions--acme (variant, profile acme)
  wrote  ingredients/rules/project-conventions--acme/ingredient.yaml
  wrote  ingredients/rules/project-conventions--acme/rule.md
  edited recipes/base.yaml (ingredients)
  the Forge is not committed — review with git, then commit and push it
```

Then three buttons, Get started (https://craftar.dev/docs/#start), Read the model, Install craftar (`npm install -g craftar`, https://craftar.dev/docs/#install), and the supported tools, each shown with its official logo and linking its official site: Claude Code, Kiro, AGENTS.md, Cursor, Copilot, Agent Skills, Codex, Antigravity, OpenCode.

## Terminology

- Harness: everything that shapes how coding agents behave in a repository, rules, agents, commands, skills, hooks, MCP servers.
- Forge: Git repository holding every ingredient, recipe and profile; read by path, or by git URL at a ref. It is never a Git remote of any team repository.
- Ingredient: smallest reusable unit, a rule, agent, command, skill, hook, MCP server, script, steering file or local service.
- Recipe: named set of ingredients with parameters; stack recipes declare a `slot`.
- Profile: one team, its recipes, targets, parameters and sections.
- Workspace: a folder with `craftar.yaml` (profile, recipe changes, targets) and a git-ignored `craftar.local.yaml` per developer.
- Target: an AI coder to emit for; the capability matrix (Targets and capability coverage, below) lists what each one gets.
- Lockfile (`craftar.lock`): the Forge's source, ref and commit and a normalized hash per generated file, the authority on what Craftar owns.
- Registry (`~/.craftar/registry.json`): every workspace synced on this machine; `craftar workspaces` and `craftar ui` show them.

The full definitions are in the documentation (https://craftar.dev/docs/).

## Problem statement

Two problems, one root: the harness has no source and no record.

### P1: One harness, T teams, K AI coders, A agents each, maintained by hand

The same agents, rules, commands, hooks and MCP servers live as T copies in K formats (`.claude/`, `.kiro/`, `AGENTS.md`, `.cursor/`). A change costs T × K manual edits, with no record of what came from what.

Requires: one source; emission per target; a record per file.

```mermaid
graph LR
  H["harness on the developer's machine · 12 rules · 7 agents · 9 commands · skills · hooks · 4 MCP servers"]
  H -->|copy and translate by hand| A["team A · Claude Code · .claude/ · two months old"]
  H -->|copy and translate by hand| B["team B · Kimi · AGENTS.md · one stale agent"]
  H -->|copy and translate by hand| C["team C · Kiro · .kiro/ · one agent missing"]
  H -->|copy and translate by hand| D["team D · Cursor · .cursor/ · version 3 of 5"]
```

State today (diagram): a single harness (about 12 rules, 7 agents, 9 commands, skills, hooks and 4 MCP servers) exists only as a folder on the developer's machine. It is copied and translated by hand into four team workspaces: team A uses Claude Code, team B uses Kimi via `AGENTS.md`, team C uses Kiro, team D uses Cursor. Because the copies are manual, they diverge: team A's copy is two months old, team B has one stale agent, team C is missing one agent, team D carries version 3 of 5. No edge in this graph is recorded anywhere, so nothing can report which copy is current.

### P2: One developer, many workspaces, separate remotes

One workspace per team, each on that team's Git host, its harness copied in by hand. Nothing records which version each one carries, or whether a file was edited in place.

Requires: a channel that is no team repository's remote; a lock per workspace; a registry.

State today (diagram): one developer machine holds four workspaces, `workspace-1` to `workspace-4`, one per team. Each workspace contains that team's repositories cloned from that team's own Git remote (four different hosts), so no repository is shared across workspaces. Each workspace also contains a hand-copied `.claude/` harness of unknown version: v3?, v2?, v5?, v4+?: copied at different times or edited in place, with no lockfile. The harness moves from one workspace to the next by hand, one copy at a time, which is how the versions drift apart. The machine has no registry of workspaces, no shared source for the harness, and no way to verify versions.

## Failure modes (observed in earlier generators and hand-synchronised workspaces)

Eight failures seen in two earlier generators and in hand-synced workspaces: FM-1 to FM-5 from P1, FM-6 to FM-8 from P2. Each becomes a constraint in Invariants.

- FM-1 Regeneration deletes hand-written agents and rules. Cause: the generator owned the whole `.claude/` folder.
- FM-2 Every file reads as hand-edited; the team lives on `--force`. Cause: raw-byte hashes; a Windows checkout rewrites LF→CRLF.
- FM-3 A deleted rule keeps loading into sessions. Cause: the generator only wrote, never removed.
- FM-4 Kiro mirrors drift 4–52 lines from their source. Cause: only rules were generated; the rest were hand mirrors.
- FM-5 A rule and its reviewer agent contradict each other. Cause: two files stating the same constraints, edited apart.
- FM-6 A model pin or MCP version breaks in three places at once. Cause: volatile values inlined instead of declared once.
- FM-7 "Everything in English" contradicted by 18 files. Cause: language treated as the workspace's, not the ingredient's.
- FM-8 Real package-feed tokens in a staged `settings.json`. Cause: settings carried values instead of variable references.

## Model: source, resolution, emission

Ingredients are source; recipes and profiles compose them; `craftar sync` resolves them for one workspace, writes each target's files and records them in a lockfile. Generated files are committed, so a team that only uses Kiro never needs Craftar installed.

Layer resolution, weakest to strongest: `base` recipe → stack recipes → team profile → `craftar.yaml` (workspace, committed) → `craftar.local.yaml` (one developer, git-ignored). The strongest layer wins; stack recipes that share a `slot` exclude each other, and `{{params}}` come from the winning layer. `craftar explain <file>` names the layer behind each output.

Pipeline of `craftar sync`:
1. Read `craftar.yaml`; load the Forge: a path, or a git URL at a ref, cached per machine.
2. Resolve layers, exclusive slots and params into the final ingredient set.
3. Emit the open standards (`AGENTS.md`, Agent Skills, `mcp.json`) through the target emitters.
4. Emit each tool's own format through one Craftar emitter per target.
5. Diff against `craftar.lock`; classify each file (new · update · unchanged · adopt · drift · collision · orphan); write, remove orphans, refresh the lock.

Targets, generated and committed: working: Claude Code (`.claude/`, `.mcp.json`); Kiro (`.kiro/steering`, `.kiro/agents/*.json`); `AGENTS.md` at the root, read by Codex, Cursor, Copilot, Antigravity, OpenCode, Warp and Kimi; Cursor (`.cursor/rules/*.mdc`, `.cursor/agents/`, `.cursor/mcp.json`); Copilot (`.github/instructions`, `.github/agents`, `.github/mcp.json`, plus `.github/prompts` and `.vscode/mcp.json` for VS Code); Agent Skills (`.agents/skills/`, read by Cursor, Copilot, Codex, Antigravity and OpenCode); Codex (`.codex/agents/*.toml`, `.codex/hooks.json`, rules through `AGENTS.md`); Antigravity (`.agents/rules`, `.agents/agents`, `.agents/mcp_config.json`, `.agents/hooks.json`). mvp: OpenCode (`.opencode/agents`, `.opencode/commands`, `.opencode/opencode.json`, rules through `AGENTS.md`). Composed files carry a `GENERATED` banner; Claude Code files are written verbatim, so an existing workspace is adopted byte for byte. What Craftar owns is recorded in `craftar.lock`.

P1 resolved (diagram): the Forge is one Git repository containing ingredients (rules, agents, commands, skills, hooks, MCP servers, scripts, steering files), recipes (`base`, `backend-*`, `frontend-*`, `aws-local`, `pm-*`) and one profile per team. Running `craftar sync` in a workspace loads the Forge (by path, or by git URL at a ref), resolves layers, emits files for each of the workspace's targets and writes `craftar.lock`. Team A emits to `.claude/` with 7 agents; team B swaps the frontend recipe and has three workspaces, one target each: `.claude/`, `.kiro/` and `AGENTS.md`, which carries the rules only; team C emits `.kiro/` and pins the Forge at tag `v2.3`, and its lock is up to date; team D sets its targets to agents-md in its local file, so Cursor reads the emitted `AGENTS.md`, which carries the rules only, and has one drifted file. Every edge is generated and recorded in the lock.

P1 resolved: solid edges are generated and recorded in each workspace's lockfile; `status` reads it to report drift per workspace.

```mermaid
graph LR
  F["Forge · one Git repository · ingredients, recipes, profiles"] --> CR["craftar · reads the Forge at its ref, emits per target"]
  CR --> W1["workspace-1 · .claude/ · craftar.lock 7c1e9a2 · up to date"]
  CR --> W2["workspace-2 · AGENTS.md · craftar.lock 7c1e9a2 · up to date"]
  CR --> W3["workspace-3 · .kiro/ · craftar.lock 5b0d3f1 · outdated, forge moved"]
  CR --> W4["workspace-4 · AGENTS.md · craftar.lock 7c1e9a2 · drift"]
  R1["team 1 Git remote"] -->|git clone| W1
  R2["team 2 Git remote"] -->|git clone| W2
  R3["team 3 Git remote"] -->|git clone| W3
  R4["team 4 Git remote"] -->|git clone| W4
  REG["~/.craftar/registry.json · read by craftar workspaces"] -.-> W1 & W2 & W3 & W4
```

P2 resolved (diagram): same developer machine and same four workspaces as the problem statement, `workspace-1` to `workspace-4`, each still cloning its team's repositories from that team's own remote. Now a fifth repository, the Forge, is referenced by each workspace's `craftar.yaml` and is not a remote of any team repository. Between them sits `craftar` itself: it reads the Forge and emits each workspace's harness, so nothing flows from the Forge to a workspace except through it. Each workspace carries a generated harness with the same base ingredients and a `craftar.lock` naming the Forge commit that produced it (`7c1e9a2` for three of them, `5b0d3f1` for the one synced before the Forge moved). Every writing sync records its workspace in the registry at `~/.craftar/registry.json`, and `craftar workspaces` reports per workspace: up to date, outdated with forge moved, or drift.

## In practice: Forge → Workspace by stack

Above, the logical flow; below, how a real Forge for one stack becomes files: pick a stack, then a target, to see what `craftar sync` writes. Every stack lists Claude Code, Kiro and AGENTS.md, and a Five more targets tab: Cursor, Copilot, Agent Skills, Codex and Antigravity in one workspace. All eight are working; the capability matrix (Targets and capability coverage, below) lists every path. In each workspace, `craftar.yaml` is the input the workspace owns and `craftar.lock` is generated.

### dotnet-enterprise: .NET backend teams following Clean Architecture

Forge structure:
- ingredients/rules/: dotnet-clean-architecture, dotnet-clean-code, dotnet-minimal-api, dotnet-entity-framework, dotnet-security
- ingredients/agents/: dotnet-arch-reviewer, dotnet-api-reviewer, dotnet-ef-reviewer, dotnet-security-reviewer
- ingredients/commands/: create-api-endpoint
- recipes/: dotnet-clean-arch.yaml
- profiles/: team-dotnet/

Workspace output (Claude Code target):
- .claude/rules/: dotnet-clean-architecture.md, dotnet-clean-code.md, dotnet-minimal-api.md, dotnet-entity-framework.md, dotnet-security.md
- .claude/agents/: dotnet-arch-reviewer.md, dotnet-api-reviewer.md, dotnet-ef-reviewer.md, dotnet-security-reviewer.md
- .claude/commands/: create-api-endpoint.md
- src/ (client code, untouched)

Workspace output (Kiro target):
- .kiro/steering/: *.md (same rules)
- .kiro/steering/commands/: create-api-endpoint.md
- .kiro/agents/: *.json (agents as JSON)

Workspace output (AGENTS.md target):
- AGENTS.md (always-on rules concatenated, then the scoped rules embedded in full: no other target writes them here)
- One file: the rules only. Everything else has no AGENTS.md form, so sync skips it and warns, naming each ingredient.

Workspace output (five more targets: cursor, copilot, agent-skills, codex, antigravity, in one workspace):
- .cursor/rules/: *.mdc; .cursor/agents/: *.md (Cursor)
- .github/copilot-instructions.md (always-on rules), .github/instructions/: *.instructions.md (scoped rules), .github/agents/: *.agent.md (Copilot)
- .codex/agents/: *.toml (Codex)
- .agents/rules/: *.md; .agents/agents/: *.md (Antigravity)
- .agents/skills/create-api-endpoint/SKILL.md (Agent Skills: the command, as a skill)
- Commands become skills under .agents/skills/, which Cursor, Copilot, Codex and Antigravity read. Codex takes the agents only and reads its rules from AGENTS.md; sync warns where Cursor and Antigravity drop an agent's `tools` and Codex its `model` and `tools`.

### node-fullstack: Node.js teams using TypeScript

Forge structure:
- ingredients/rules/: node-typescript-strict, node-express-patterns, node-testing-jest, node-eslint-prettier, node-security-headers
- ingredients/agents/: node-arch-reviewer, node-api-reviewer, node-test-reviewer, node-deps-reviewer
- ingredients/commands/: create-express-route
- ingredients/mcp/: npm-audit
- recipes/: node-express-ts.yaml
- profiles/: team-node/

Workspace output (Claude Code target):
- .claude/rules/, .claude/agents/, .claude/commands/
- .mcp.json (npm-audit MCP)

Workspace output (Kiro target):
- .kiro/steering/: *.md, with .kiro/steering/commands/create-express-route.md
- .kiro/agents/: *.json
- .kiro/settings/mcp.json (npm-audit MCP)

Workspace output (AGENTS.md target):
- AGENTS.md (always-on rules concatenated, then the scoped rules embedded in full: no other target writes them here)
- One file: the rules only. Everything else has no AGENTS.md form, so sync skips it and warns, naming each ingredient.

Workspace output (five more targets: cursor, copilot, agent-skills, codex, antigravity, in one workspace):
- .cursor/rules/: *.mdc; .cursor/agents/: *.md; .cursor/mcp.json (npm-audit MCP) (Cursor)
- .github/copilot-instructions.md (always-on rules), .github/instructions/: *.instructions.md (scoped rules), .github/agents/: *.agent.md; .github/mcp.json (npm-audit MCP, for the Copilot CLI); .vscode/mcp.json (npm-audit MCP, for VS Code) (Copilot)
- .codex/agents/: *.toml (Codex)
- .agents/rules/: *.md; .agents/agents/: *.md; .agents/mcp_config.json (npm-audit MCP) (Antigravity)
- .agents/skills/create-express-route/SKILL.md (Agent Skills: the command, as a skill)
- Commands become skills under .agents/skills/, which Cursor, Copilot, Codex and Antigravity read. Codex takes the agents only and reads its rules from AGENTS.md; sync warns where Cursor and Antigravity drop an agent's `tools` and Codex its `model` and `tools`. Copilot writes the npm-audit server twice, for the Copilot CLI and for VS Code; Codex writes no MCP file, so sync warns and the server goes in .codex/config.toml by hand.

### iac-multicloud: Platform teams managing infrastructure as code

Forge structure:
- ingredients/rules/: aws-cloudformation, aws-cdk-typescript, azure-arm-bicep, kubernetes-helm, terraform-modules
- ingredients/agents/: aws-yaml-reviewer, azure-iac-reviewer, k8s-manifest-reviewer, terraform-reviewer
- ingredients/commands/: create-aws-stack, create-helm-chart
- recipes/: iac-aws.yaml, iac-kubernetes.yaml
- profiles/: team-platform/

Workspace output (Claude Code target):
- .claude/rules/: aws-cloudformation.md, aws-cdk-typescript.md, azure-arm-bicep.md, kubernetes-helm.md, terraform-modules.md
- .claude/agents/, .claude/commands/
- infra/ (client IaC, untouched)

Workspace output (Kiro target):
- .kiro/steering/: *.md, with .kiro/steering/commands/: *.md
- .kiro/agents/: *.json

Workspace output (AGENTS.md target):
- AGENTS.md (always-on rules concatenated, then the scoped rules embedded in full: no other target writes them here)
- One file: the rules only. Everything else has no AGENTS.md form, so sync skips it and warns, naming each ingredient.

Workspace output (five more targets: cursor, copilot, agent-skills, codex, antigravity, in one workspace):
- .cursor/rules/: *.mdc; .cursor/agents/: *.md (Cursor)
- .github/copilot-instructions.md (always-on rules), .github/instructions/: *.instructions.md (scoped rules), .github/agents/: *.agent.md (Copilot)
- .codex/agents/: *.toml (Codex)
- .agents/rules/: *.md; .agents/agents/: *.md (Antigravity)
- .agents/skills/create-aws-stack/SKILL.md, .agents/skills/create-helm-chart/SKILL.md (Agent Skills: each command, as a skill)
- Commands become skills under .agents/skills/, which Cursor, Copilot, Codex and Antigravity read. Codex takes the agents only and reads its rules from AGENTS.md; sync warns where Cursor and Antigravity drop an agent's `tools` and Codex its `model` and `tools`.

### What syncs where

Craftar writes only each AI coder's own files (every path is in the capability matrix) and a root `AGENTS.md`, read by Codex, Cursor, Copilot, Antigravity, OpenCode, Warp and Kimi; plus `.craftar/` when the recipes bring a local service. Folders like `src/` or `infra/` are never touched: only paths recorded in `craftar.lock` are written or removed. Outside the workspace and the Forge it writes only under `~/.craftar`: the Forge cache and the registry.

### Growing the Forge: a second client, one base

A second client imported into the Forge reuses every ingredient that matches; the ones that differ become variants named after the profile, so both workspaces still reproduce byte for byte. `forge variants` lists them, `forge diff` classifies each hunk, and `forge unify` resolves one, keep a side, move a differing value into the profile as a parameter, or a block as a section, after planning every registered workspace that reads the Forge.

Unification (diagram): the Forge already holds `rule/deploy`, whose text reads "use globex-api here". Importing a second client, `acme`, whose copy reads "use acme-api here", keeps the base and adds a variant, `rule/deploy--acme`, that emits under the original name. `craftar forge diff rule/deploy` shows one hunk, `globex-api` against `acme-api`, and suggests the class `value`. `craftar forge unify rule/deploy --profile acme --plan plan.yaml`, with that hunk set to `take: param` and the key `deploy.api`, rewrites the base to "use {{deploy.api}} here", declares `globex-api` as the key's default in the base's `ingredient.yaml`, writes `deploy.api: acme-api` into `profiles/acme/profile.yaml` and removes the variant. Every path it overwrites or deletes must be held by git. Re-importing `acme` afterwards compares its file with the base as sync renders it for `acme`, finds them equal and reuses the base: no variant, no change to the profile.

One rule, two clients. `forge unify` refuses when another layer, profile or ingredient already uses the key; `forge promote` makes a profile's variant the base.

## Get going (as on https://craftar.dev/docs/, Start here #start, Install #install, Setup #setup, Forges #forges)

### Start here

craftar keeps one AI-coding harness (rules, agents, commands, skills, hooks and MCP servers) in a Git repository, the Forge, and writes each tool's own files from it into every workspace, recording them in `craftar.lock`. Import first: `craftar import` turns an existing workspace into a Forge and a `craftar.yaml`, and `craftar diff` proves nothing would change. Then add targets and run `craftar sync`. No Forge yet? See Setup.

Terminal (animated on the page; craftar 1.6.0 on a synthetic workspace, the file list shortened (the run wrote 22 files), the run's scratch home shown as ~, and the # line standing for the edit that adds the targets to craftar.yaml):

```
$ craftar import --from claude-code --forge ../acme-forge --profile acme --write-config
Imported ~/work/acme-api → ~/work/acme-forge as profile "acme"
  10 created, 0 reused, 0 variants, 0 rejected
  profile profiles/acme/profile.yaml created
  recipes: base
$ craftar diff
no differences
$ # craftar.yaml: targets: [claude-code, kiro, agents-md, cursor, opencode]
$ craftar sync
craftar sync — profile acme · recipes base · targets claude-code, kiro, agents-md, cursor, opencode
  wrote 22, removed 0 orphan(s), skipped 0
  + .claude/rules/workflow.md
  + .cursor/agents/docs-author.md
  + .kiro/steering/workflow.md
  + .opencode/agents/docs-author.md
  + .opencode/opencode.json
  + AGENTS.md
```

How byte fidelity is checked: the oracle imports a hand-built workspace (Claude Code + Kiro), syncs it and asserts every generated file byte for byte, then that a second sync is a no-op, a hand edit survives as drift and a removed ingredient disappears.

### Install

Needs Node 22 or later, and git for a Forge in a repository. `npx craftar --version` runs any command through npx; `craftar doctor` lists what is off on the machine and in the workspace, with the fix.

```
$ npm install -g craftar
$ craftar --version
1.8.0
```

Stack: TypeScript/Node CLI (commander, zod, yaml) with its own emitter per target; rulesync stays a reference for the formats, not a dependency. License: MIT.

craftar for Orca, the Orca plugin, released as 0.1.0 (https://github.com/llima/craftar-orca#install); its README says how to install it and what approving it grants.

### Setup: a new Forge and its first workspaces (since 1.7.0)

`craftar setup` creates a Forge (a new Git repository with one commit) and starts the first workspaces on it. It needs craftar 1.7.0 or later; with a Forge already, start a workspace with `craftar init --forge <dir> --profile <name>`. `craftar setup` alone, in a terminal, asks where the Forge goes, its first profile, the workspaces and the targets; `--import` brings a workspace's `.claude/` into the new Forge first. Setup only creates: a Forge directory that exists and is not empty is refused, with the `craftar init` command to use it instead. The Forge gets a README, a starter rule, the profile and a `base` recipe, and one commit with no remote; each workspace then gets its `craftar.yaml` and its first sync. The interactive form lists every target, each as working or mvp, and ends with the `craftar setup` line that repeats it.

Terminal (animated on the page; measured on the 1.7.0 branch, llima/craftar-cli#130; the commit hash differs on every run):

```
$ craftar setup --forge-dir acme-forge --profile acme --targets claude-code,kiro --workspace acme-portal
craftar setup — created Forge acme-forge at /work/acme-forge (schema 1)
  wrote craftar.forge.yaml, README.md, ingredients/rules/project-conventions/ingredient.yaml, ingredients/rules/project-conventions/rule.md, profiles/acme/profile.yaml, recipes/base.yaml
  git: initial commit 04b6cbb (no remote)
craftar init — wrote craftar.yaml in /work/acme-portal
  forge ../acme-forge · profile acme · recipes base · targets claude-code, kiro (from the profile)
craftar sync — profile acme · recipes base · targets claude-code, kiro
  wrote 2, removed 0 orphan(s), skipped 0
  + .claude/rules/project-conventions.md
  + .kiro/steering/project-conventions.md
next: edit the Forge (/work/acme-forge), commit, then craftar sync in each workspace
```

### Forges

A Forge is one Git repository holding every ingredient, recipe and profile. Workspaces point at it by path, or by git URL at a branch, tag or full SHA; it is never a remote of a team repository. Layout: `craftar.forge.yaml` (schema 1 … 18, each level opt-in); `ingredients/<type>/<name>/` (an `ingredient.yaml` plus its files, rules, agents, commands, skills, hooks, mcp, scripts, steering, services); `recipes/` (`base.yaml`, stack recipes with a slot); `profiles/<name>/profile.yaml` (recipes, targets, params, sections). `craftar recipes --forge <dir>` lists the recipes and the profiles that use them, `craftar ingredients --forge <dir>` every ingredient with its type and targets, `craftar forge variants --forge <dir>` where clients differ. A recipe bundles ingredients with parameters; a profile (one per client) picks recipes, targets and values. A second client imported into the same Forge reuses what matches and makes the rest variants, which `forge unify` folds back (see Growing the Forge and F2). A Forge declares the `schema:` it needs, and an older craftar refuses a level it does not know.

## Capabilities (F1–F12: the home lists the twelve, each linking its entry; in full as on https://craftar.dev/docs/, entry F<n> is #f<n> there; "working" = runs today and is covered by tests; "mvp" = first release (on a target, as for OpenCode in the matrix: loaded by the tool, not yet used by a model session); "planned" = designed, not built)

- F1 Forge → workspace sync [working, mvp] (P1, P2): `craftar sync [--dry-run] [--check] [--overwrite-drift]`, `diff [--exit-code]` (what sync would change, an orphan shown as the removal of the whole file, a hand-edited one as a header; with `--exit-code`, exit 1 exactly when `sync --check` would fail), `status` (per file: new, update, unchanged, adopt, drift, collision, orphan, orphan-drift); sync prints what it wrote, removed and skipped, file by file. With a git-URL Forge, `ref` follows a branch or pins a tag or full SHA; sync fetches first and fails when it cannot, so CI never syncs from a stale copy unless it passes `--offline`, which reads the cached copy. `craftar cache prune [--dry-run]` removes the Forge cache entries nothing uses (no registered workspace and not the current one) entries whose first fetch never completed, and trees unused for 14 days; it never touches a workspace, a lock or the registry, and `--dry-run` shows what it would remove. A symbolic link never carries `sync` out of the tree it works on: a Forge file read through a link that leaves the Forge or leads into its `.git`, and a workspace path that leaves through one, refuse the run before anything is written, there is no flag; a link that stays inside works as before. In a git repository, `sync` and `sync --check` warn for each generated file git ignores, naming the ignore rule by file, line and pattern; craftar never edits an ignore file, and `mayBeIgnored` in `craftar.yaml` lists the paths kept out of git on purpose. Planned: `--targets`, `update`.
- F2 Multi-target emission [working, mvp] (P1): `craftar import --from claude-code`; Craftar's own emitters for Claude Code, Kiro (byte-identical to a hand-built workspace, including agent JSON and command mirrors) and AGENTS.md (working) and, since 1.1.0 and 1.2.0, Cursor, Copilot, Agent Skills (`.agents/skills/`), Codex and Antigravity, working since 1.5.0, validated on 2026-11-07 by opening each tool from its CLI on a synthetic workspace, and, since 1.6.0, OpenCode, mvp: agents to `.opencode/agents/` with permissions derived from their tools, commands to `.opencode/commands/` and MCP servers to `.opencode/opencode.json`, its rules through `AGENTS.md`; OpenCode 2.2.5 loaded them through its local service, with no model, and it stays mvp until a model session uses those files. Copilot writes its MCP servers to `.vscode/mcp.json` for VS Code and to `.github/mcp.json` for the Copilot CLI; `.github/prompts/` is VS Code's, and the Copilot CLI reads commands from `.agents/skills/`. Codex reads `.codex/agents/` only in a trusted project, and `.codex/hooks.json` only once its hooks were reviewed, and Antigravity run headless never applied a `glob` rule; post-processors for gaps (e.g. Kiro agent `resources` and `permissions`). Importing a second client into an existing Forge reuses every ingredient whose render for that profile equals the workspace file, infers declared `{{key}}` values into the profile, and makes the rest variants; `craftar forge variants` (where clients differ, nearest first), `craftar forge diff <type/name>` (hunks, each with a suggested class) and `craftar forge unify <type/name> --profile <p> --plan <file>` (base, variant, param or section) resolve each one back into its base (see Growing the Forge); `craftar forge promote <type/name> --profile <p>` goes the other way: it makes a profile's variant the base and gives the old base back, as a variant of its own, to every other profile that resolved it, gated on git, proved before the first write, never a commit; `craftar forge impact` lists every registered workspace reading this Forge and what its next sync would do; `craftar targets` prints the capability matrix: what each target does with each ingredient type. `craftar import --report <file.md>` also writes a Markdown report of the import: what was created, reused, made a variant or rejected, and the `.kiro/` files that differ from what `sync` would generate, as paths and line counts, never content. `craftar import --prefer-kiro <rule,…>` takes the named rules from `.kiro/steering/<name>.md` instead of `.claude/rules/<name>.md`, for a steering mirror that was edited by hand and is the text to keep; the text is accepted only when it is proved to render back to that steering file's body for Kiro. Rules only: commands, agents and skills are not taken from Kiro. Import reads a Claude rule's `paths:` frontmatter as its scope, so a scoped rule stays scoped (`fileMatch` for Kiro, and a scoped rule in `AGENTS.md`) and keeps that frontmatter verbatim, so `.claude/rules/<name>.md` comes back byte for byte. At `schema: 7` import never writes a generated rules index over its placeholder silently: a variant that holds the placeholder and whose file differs from what `sync` writes is refused, a new variant that freezes the list is warned, and `--prefer-kiro` refuses a rule whose ingredient holds the placeholder. Import takes nothing from behind a symbolic link that leaves the workspace or leads into its `.git`: such a source is rejected and listed, never adopted. In a Forge at `schema: 8`, a source equal to the importing profile's own local is reused there, one that differs is refused, and the Forge it would write is first loaded on a scratch copy. With `--local=auto`, a new source of the profile becomes a local there instead of a root ingredient, and a local that differs is rewritten; `--local=always` writes no ingredient at the root. A new local no recipe of the profile's folder cites is wired into the recipe `<p>-local`. With `agents-md.primary: true`, in a Forge that declares `schema: 5` and a workspace whose targets include `agents-md`, an always-on rule with the default `targets` is written to `AGENTS.md` alone, with all three targets, instead of three times (`.claude/rules/`, `.kiro/steering/` and `AGENTS.md`): its other files become orphans `sync` removes; the `.claude/`, `.kiro/` and `AGENTS.md` texts that cite it point at its place in `AGENTS.md`; scripts, hooks and files copied as bytes are never rewritten: a reference left there is warned with its file and line; and generated Kiro `resources` name only the steering files the plan writes, while a hand-written entry naming a file the plan does not write and the disk lacks fails `sync --check` (a writing `sync` still writes). Craftar writes no `CLAUDE.md`; when one keeps Claude Code from reading `AGENTS.md`, every plan says so. The mode is opt-in (a workspace that does not set it sees no change) and every craftar before 0.36.0 refuses a `schema: 5` Forge. A `hook` ingredient can declare its `registration` (the event, matcher and command Claude Code runs it with) and `claude-code` writes it to `.claude/settings.craftar.example.json`; `craftar settings apply` merges it into `.claude/settings.json`, only when a person types it, keeping every `env` value, `permissions` and every other key: or the block is copied by hand. No other command writes a settings file Claude Code reads. Every craftar before 0.38.0 refuses a Forge whose hook holds `registration`. What a tool already reads in another target's file is not written twice: with `agents-md` among the targets, an always-on rule with the default `targets` is left to `AGENTS.md` by Cursor, Copilot and Antigravity, and with `agent-skills`, a command with the default `targets` is left to `.agents/skills/` by Copilot; `craftar explain` on such a file names the file that holds it. A Forge file that names `cursor`, `copilot` or `agent-skills` in `targets` needs `schema: 15`, one that names `codex` or `antigravity` needs `schema: 16`, and one that names `opencode` needs `schema: 18`; a workspace may name any of them in `craftar.yaml` at any Forge schema. Since 1.3.0 a `hook` ingredient with a `registration` is written for Codex to `.codex/hooks.json` and for Antigravity to `.agents/hooks.json`; Cursor, the Copilot CLI and VS Code run the hooks `.claude/settings.json` holds, so no file of theirs is written. rulesync stays a reference for the formats, not a dependency.
- F3 Layers and stack slots [working] (P1): layer resolution, exclusive slots, params, `explain`; `craftar.local.yaml` (git-ignored) overrides the workspace for one developer, its arrays replacing the workspace's; sections, a client-specific block in an ingredient body marked `<!-- craftar:section flavors -->` … `<!-- /craftar:section -->`, whose content is the default and which a profile's `sections` or the workspace's `overrides.sections` replace or empty, with no rendered body holding the markers and `explain` naming the layer each came from; `forge unify` can extract one from a variant (`take: section`); a Forge that uses sections declares `schema: 2` or above, so an older CLI refuses it rather than leak the markers. In a Forge that declares `schema: 6`, an opening marker can name the targets that receive the block (`<!-- craftar:section flavors targets=claude-code,kiro -->`): a target it names gets the section as any other, a target it does not name gets nothing of it, whatever a profile or the workspace sets, and a marker with no `targets=` is read as before. A Forge that writes no `targets=` sees no change, and every craftar before 0.39.0 refuses a `schema: 6` Forge. In a Forge that declares `schema: 7`, a line of a rule or steering body that holds `{{craftar.rules.index}}` alone becomes the list of the rules the profile resolves, as each target names them: up to three groups (`Always on:`, `Scoped:`, `On request:`) one line per rule with its description, or by its reference alone, warned, when it has none; a rule no target of the workspace writes is left out. `explain` names an indexed file's list, `AGENTS.md` aside. A placeholder not alone on its line, or in an agent, a command or a skill, is left as written and warned; so is one alone on its line below `schema: 7`. Either warning makes `doctor --strict` exit 1. The index is generated, never a parameter, and every key starting with `craftar.` is reserved: `forge unify` never extracts into one and `import` never infers one. A Forge that writes no placeholder and sets no `craftar.` key sees no change from the index, and every craftar before 0.40.0 refuses a `schema: 7` Forge. In a Forge that declares `schema: 8`, a profile's folder holds its own ingredients and recipes (`profiles/<p>/ingredients/`, `profiles/<p>/recipes/`), which only that profile sees: they render exactly as they would at the root, a root recipe can never reach them, and a broken reference fails the load, naming the files. `explain` names where a file's ingredient lives. Every craftar before 0.45.0 refuses a `schema: 8` Forge. `craftar forge localize` moves a root ingredient only one profile resolves into that profile's folder, with the root recipes that cite it, and `craftar forge share` moves a local back to the root: each gated on git and proved, before the first write, to change no byte any profile or registered workspace plans; neither commits. In a Forge that declares `schema: 9`, an ingredient's metadata takes `{{param}}` too (a rule's `paths:` and pattern, an agent's or a command's description) a value that would break the file it lands in fails the plan, and `forge diff` and `forge unify` work on those fields; every craftar before 0.47.0 refuses a `schema: 9` Forge. `craftar recipes` and `craftar ingredients` list the whole Forge read-only, mark what the workspace uses (and, for recipes, why), and `--recipe` shows what choosing one would bring. `craftar add recipe` and `craftar remove recipe` change the workspace's choice in `craftar.yaml` in place, refusing a recipe that would share a slot (unless `--replace`), removing one another recipe still brings in through `extends`, or an edit that would not resolve, and print what the next `sync` would do; they never sync.
- F4 Workspace bootstrap [working] (P2): `craftar init --forge <dir|url> --profile <name>` (with `--targets`, `--add-recipe`, `--remove-recipe`, `--clone`; `--new-profile <name> [--like <profile>]` in place of `--profile`) writes `craftar.yaml` (the Forge, the profile, and the recipe and target choices, given as flags or as answers) only once the workspace resolves and plans, then runs the first `sync`, which registers the workspace; files already on disk are adopted when they equal the plan and otherwise left as they are and reported; an existing `craftar.yaml` is never edited. In a terminal, `craftar init` asks for a `--forge` or a `--profile` it was not given, the Forge last synced on this machine offered, the profile from the Forge's list, then the recipes and targets to keep or adjust, confirms once before anything is written, and ends by printing the same run as flags, for CI; off a terminal a missing flag is refused. When a declared parameter a file the plan writes cites has no value, `craftar.yaml` is still written and the first `sync` is not run. With `--clone` it then clones each repository the profile's `repos` lists into the workspace: `git clone` over `https` or `ssh` only, with the `git` found on `PATH`, never over a file `sync` writes, into the Forge or out of the workspace; when `init` asks for what the flags do not give, it lists the URLs first and asks, the default no. A clone is recorded nowhere, and `sync` never updates or removes it. `craftar repos` lists those repositories in an existing workspace (`present`, `missing` or `blocked`, with their URLs) and `craftar repos clone` clones the missing ones. With `--new-profile <name>` (optionally `--like <profile>`), `init` first writes one new file in a Forge directory, `profiles/<name>/profile.yaml` (the recipes and targets chosen, nothing else of the template) behind a git gate and never committed, then starts the workspace on it; in a terminal the profile list offers `0) a new profile`.
- F5 PM tool and internal platform per profile [working] (P1): in a Forge that declares `schema: 3` or above, a profile's `integrations` block selects recipes and gives params. `integrations.<slot>.kind: <kind>` selects the recipe named `<slot>-<kind>`, `integrations.pm.kind: azure-devops` selects `pm-azure-devops`, a recipe that lists, say, the MCP ingredient and a rule describing where stories live, and every scalar of the block is the param `integrations.<slot>.<key>`, cited in a body as `{{integrations.pm.org}}`. An integration with no `kind` gives params only. A schema 3 Forge is read only by craftar 0.27.0 and later; below `schema: 3` the block is ignored, without a warning; a `kind` with no recipe stops `sync`. In a Forge that declares `schema: 4`, an MCP server takes the params its ingredient declares, so one server serves every client: `url: "{{integrations.idp.url}}"`, with `integrations.idp.url` declared in the ingredient's `params`, renders each profile's own URL, and `.mcp.json` and `.kiro/settings/mcp.json` get the same rendered server. A declared key with no value stops `sync`; a key the ingredient does not declare is left as written, with a warning when some layer gives it a value; below `schema: 4` a server is written exactly as the Forge holds it. A schema 4 Forge is read only by craftar 0.28.0 and later. Tokens are referenced by `authEnv`, never stored (FM-8).
- F6 Local services per workspace [working] (P1): `craftar services up | down | status`. A `service` ingredient is a Docker Compose fragment plus the files it mounts. `sync` writes it under `.craftar/services/<name>/`, with the stack `.craftar/compose.yaml` (a Compose `include` of every fragment) for no target, text always LF without a BOM (a file listed as `binary` is copied as bytes), and records each file in `craftar.lock` (schema 3 only for a workspace that has a service). They are generated files like any other: `status`, `diff` and `sync --check` treat them the same. `craftar services up` reads the lock, not the Forge, and refuses to start a stack with a missing or hand-edited file, or with a stack or fragment the lock does not record; `down` stops it and `status` shows it. `sync` never runs Docker; `up` needs Docker Compose 2.20.0 or later. A Forge that holds a `service` ingredient is read only by craftar 0.25.0 and later.
- F7 Project templates [list | install working] (P1): `craftar templates list | install`. A profile's `templates` block lists packages per kind (`dotnet-new` today) with an optional `source` feed. `craftar templates list` shows what the profile declares; `craftar templates install` runs `dotnet new install` once per entry, into the user's own template store. Nothing installs implicitly: not `sync`, not `init`, not `doctor`. An entry of a kind this CLI cannot install (`npm-create`, `nx`) is listed, skipped and warned. A `source` carrying a user or a password is refused; authentication is NuGet's. Planned: a generated rule mapping archetype → template, and a wrapping `/create-project` command.
- F8 Drift and reverse contribution [working] (P2): `status` reports drift; never overwritten without `--overwrite-drift`. `craftar drift show` lists the hand-edited files, whether the Forge also changed each and whether the edit can be promoted: with a path, its diff; `craftar drift discard <path...>` is a `sync` that also regenerates the named hand-edited files (their edits are lost) and removes a named hand-edited file the Forge no longer produces; `craftar drift promote <path>` carries one hand edit of a `.claude/` file into the Forge's working tree, a value in the profile's `params` or `sections` when the edit is only that, otherwise a variant for the workspace's profile, gated on git and proved before the first write; it never syncs and never commits. A file that holds an expanded rules index is not promotable: edit the Forge's rule, or the description of the rules it lists. So is a hand edit of a metadata field the Forge renders from a parameter, at `schema: 9`; `drift show` says why. At `schema: 8`, a hand edit of a profile-local file is promoted into the local itself: a value inference proves goes to the profile's `params` or `sections`, otherwise the local's own files are edited in place, with no variant.
- F9 CI [working] (P2): `craftar sync --check`; `craftar diff --exit-code` gives the same verdict with the diff that explains it; `craftar sync --check --committed [rev]` and `--check --index` run the same check over a commit or git's index; `craftar git-hooks install [--pre-push] [--pre-commit]` writes an optional hook that runs it; the GitHub Action is `uses: llima/craftar-cli/ci/github@<SHA or v-tag>`, the Azure Pipelines template `ci/azure/check.yml@craftar`. `AGENTS.md` has a byte budget, `agents-md.maxBytes` (default 32768, Codex's `project_doc_max_bytes`; `0` turns it off): over it every plan warns, naming the largest rules, and when a recipe, the profile or the workspace sets it, `sync --check`, `status` and `diff --exit-code` with no path fail, a writing `sync` still writes. Two thin wrappers in the CLI's repository make a pull request fail when a workspace is out of step with its Forge: a GitHub Action (`ci/github/action.yml`) and an Azure Pipelines step template (`ci/azure/check.yml`). Each installs an exact `craftar` version, outside the checkout, runs `sync --check` (its exit code is the step's) and names the files out of sync as annotations and a job summary, never a file's content; they write nothing to the workspace. A private Forge's token comes only from the workflow, for an origin the workflow names. Pin them to a commit SHA or a `v<version>` tag: a change under `ci/` reaches a branch reference the moment it merges. The action ran on GitHub's Linux and Windows runners; the Azure template has not run on a real agent. `craftar sync --check --committed [rev]` and `--check --index` give the same verdict over what git holds (a commit or the index) instead of the folder, writing nothing and starting no hook, filter or `core.fsmonitor` of the repository. `craftar git-hooks install` writes, only when typed, a `pre-push` (or `pre-commit`) hook that runs that check, only inside the repository, starting only the `craftar` on `PATH`; `uninstall` and `status` complete it.
- F10 Registry and dashboard [working] (P2): a writing `sync` records its workspace in `~/.craftar/registry.json`; `craftar workspaces [--fetch]` prints each one (profile, stack, targets, Forge, last sync) with a status computed on the spot (`up to date`, `outdated`, `drift`, `no lock`, `missing` or `error`, plus `forge moved` when the Forge's commit is no longer the lock's), reading a remote Forge from the cache unless `--fetch` is given; `craftar workspaces forget <dir>` and `prune` remove entries; `CRAFTAR_NO_REGISTRY` turns the registry off, for CI runners and throwaway checkouts. From the Forge's side, `craftar forge impact` lists every registered workspace that reads it (by its path, by a git remote, or through another clone) with what its next `sync` would do; a workspace synced on CI, on another machine or with the registry off is not in it. `craftar ui [--port <n>] [--allow-writes]` serves these views as a local page in a browser: the table of `craftar workspaces` and, for a registered workspace, what `status`, `diff` and `explain` say about it and what `recipes` and `ingredients` say about its Forge. Without `--allow-writes` it is read-only: it writes nothing (the Forge cache is used as every reader uses it) and never runs `sync`: it prints the command to copy. It reaches no network either way: a remote Forge is read from the cached copy, and the page says so. Started with `--allow-writes` (typing the flag is the consent) the page also offers Sync for a workspace and Discard edit for one hand-edited file (`drift` or `orphan-drift`, from its open diff), each confirmed in the page: a sync that never passes `--overwrite-drift` (every hand edit and collision is skipped and listed) or a `craftar drift discard` of that one path. Neither is offered for `.claude/settings.craftar.example.json` or for a workspace whose Forge is remote, and either is refused when the workspace changed since the page showed it. It listens on `127.0.0.1` only (port 4747 by default; `--port 0` takes a free one), answers `GET` only (with `--allow-writes`, also `POST` to its two writing routes, from its own address) and every answer that carries data needs a token generated for that run, carried in the address it prints: whoever holds that address can read what the reading commands print, so open it only in a browser of the same user on the same machine, exactly as printed. It takes no `--workspace`, and exits 1 when the registry is off or cannot be read. `craftar ls` stays the view of the recipes and ingredients resolved for one workspace.
- F11 Craftar as an MCP server [working] (P1, P2): `craftar mcp [--workspace <dir>] [--fetch] [--allow-writes]` is an MCP server the AI coder starts, over stdin and stdout, registered in its own MCP configuration, or for a whole team as an ordinary `mcp` ingredient that `sync` writes like any other server. It serves the one workspace it was started in through seven tools that only read (`status`, `diff`, `explain`, `recipes`, `ingredients`, `targets`, `doctor`) each answering with the data its command prints, so the agent can say "run `craftar sync`" instead of editing a generated file. Without `--allow-writes` it writes nothing, no workspace file, lock, registry or Forge (the Forge cache is used as every reader uses it), reads no network unless started with `--fetch`, and never returns a hand-edited MCP configuration file; a result can carry the Forge's profile names, so register it only where that is acceptable. Started with `--allow-writes`, it also serves `sync`, `add_recipe` and `remove_recipe`. The flag grants nothing by itself: a writing call acts only in a workspace where a person typed `craftar mcp allow-writes` in a terminal, for the Forge, ref and profile the server is pinned to, the shell tools of Claude Code and Kiro give a program no terminal, so an agent cannot grant it through them (one that drives a real terminal could), and `craftar mcp revoke-writes` takes it back without a restart. The `sync` tool never overwrites or removes a hand edit: every `drift`, `orphan-drift` and `collision` is skipped and listed, for a person to resolve with `drift discard` or `drift promote`, and a remote Forge needs `--fetch`; `add_recipe` and `remove_recipe` never sync. A result carries what the commands print, never a file's content. Upgrade every machine to craftar 0.29.0 or later before adding it to a shared Forge, and to 0.35.0 or later before registering it with `--allow-writes`. In Claude Code, a plugin in the CLI's repository (`/plugin marketplace add llima/craftar-cli`, then `/plugin install craftar@craftar`) holds a `/craftar` skill and starts the `craftar` on `PATH` (install 0.40.1 or later) as `craftar mcp` with its reading tools only: never `--allow-writes`, never `--fetch`; in a project with no `craftar.yaml` it does not start. When `craftar` comes from a version manager's shim (asdf, volta, mise once trusted), a project's files can choose what runs when the server starts. Planned: an Agent Plugin.
- F12 Diagnostics [working] (P2): `craftar doctor [--fetch] [--strict] [--json]` and `craftar docs validate [path] [--fetch] [--strict] [--json]`. `craftar doctor` checks this machine (Node ≥ 22, `git`, `~/.craftar`, the registry, the Forge cache) and, inside a workspace, its configuration and Forge, the plan's warnings, declared parameters with no value (an `error` when a file the plan writes cites one, a `warn` when nothing does), the variables a written MCP server declares in `authEnv` or references as `${NAME}` and the environment lacks (names only, never values), the lock, `status` and registration, and (in a workspace with a local service) Docker with its Compose plugin and the variables a service fragment needs that nothing sets (names only), and (when the profile declares templates) the `templates` block and, for a `dotnet-new` entry, the .NET SDK (and the planned `AGENTS.md` against its byte budget) and, under `agents-md.primary`, a `CLAUDE.md`, `CLAUDE.local.md` or `.claude/CLAUDE.md` (at the root or in a directory above it) that keeps Claude Code from reading `AGENTS.md` and the Kiro agents' hand-written `resources`, and, when the plan writes a hook's registration, a planned handler that is in no settings file Claude Code reads (at most a `warn`, so `--strict` exits 1 until `craftar settings apply` runs or the block is copied), and, when `claude-code` writes a skill as one file, that Claude Code (measured with `2.1.310`) does not list it (a `warn` per skill, with the fix, so `--strict` exits 1; the file is still written), and, in a git repository, a generated file git ignores (`generated-ignored`, a `warn`, unless the path is listed under `mayBeIgnored`), and a hook `craftar git-hooks` wrote (`git-hooks`): and a path that leaves the workspace through a symbolic link (`workspace-links`, an `error`); each finding is one line (`ok`, `warn` or `error`) with the command that fixes it; it only reports (nothing is written to a workspace, a lock or the registry) and reads a remote Forge from the cache unless `--fetch` is given; it exits 1 on an `error`, or on a `warn` under `--strict`; `--json` is a contract for tooling. `craftar docs validate` checks a workspace's Markdown under `docs/`, `.claude/` and at its root, links that resolve inside the workspace, tool-call tags leaked outside code, files that are not UTF-8 text and, where the profile declares a `docs:` block, its categories, required frontmatter, dated file names and `related:` entries, one line per finding, naming a file, a line and a column, never a line of the file; it writes nothing and reads without the network unless `--fetch`, which concerns the Forge only.

## Targets and capability coverage (as on https://craftar.dev/docs/#targets)

`craftar targets` prints the capability matrix from the CLI's own table, and `sync` skips by it: with a warning that names the ingredient, never silently. Three words. Native: written in the tool's own place for that type, as the Forge holds it; converted: written in another form (frontmatter or a banner added, references rewritten, another container format, or folded into a shared file); unsupported: not written, sync warns and names the ingredient. The five targets after the first three were validated on 2026-11-07 by opening each tool on a workspace craftar synced; `opencode`, new in 1.6.0, is mvp.

Working: claude-code, kiro, agents-md, cursor, copilot, agent-skills, codex, antigravity; mvp: opencode:

| ingredient type | claude-code | kiro | agents-md | cursor | copilot | agent-skills | codex | antigravity | opencode (mvp) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| rule | native (`.claude/rules/<name>.md`) | converted (`.kiro/steering/<name>.md`) | converted (`AGENTS.md`) | converted (`.cursor/rules/<name>.mdc`) | converted (`.github/instructions/<name>.instructions.md` and `.github/copilot-instructions.md`) | unsupported | unsupported (through agents-md) | converted (`.agents/rules/<name>.md`) | unsupported (through agents-md) |
| agent | native (`.claude/agents/<name>.md`) | converted (`.kiro/agents/<name>.json`) | unsupported | converted (`.cursor/agents/<name>.md`) | converted (`.github/agents/<name>.agent.md`) | unsupported | converted (`.codex/agents/<name>.toml`) | converted (`.agents/agents/<name>.md`) | converted (`.opencode/agents/<name>.md`) |
| command | native (`.claude/commands/<name>.md`) | converted (`.kiro/steering/commands/<name>.md`) | unsupported | unsupported (through agent-skills) | converted (`.github/prompts/<name>.prompt.md`) | converted (`.agents/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`) | unsupported (through agent-skills) | unsupported (through agent-skills) | converted (`.opencode/commands/<name>.md`) |
| skill | native (`.claude/skills/<name>/<file>` or `.claude/skills/<name>.md`) | converted (`.kiro/skills/<name>/<file>`) | unsupported | unsupported (through agent-skills) | unsupported (through agent-skills) | converted (`.agents/skills/<name>/<file>`) | unsupported (through agent-skills) | unsupported (through agent-skills) | unsupported (through agent-skills) |
| mcp | native (`.mcp.json` and `.claude/settings.craftar.example.json`) | native (`.kiro/settings/mcp.json`) | unsupported | converted (`.cursor/mcp.json`) | converted (`.vscode/mcp.json` and `.github/mcp.json`) | unsupported | unsupported (configure `.codex/config.toml` by hand) | converted (`.agents/mcp_config.json`) | converted (`.opencode/opencode.json`) |
| script | native (`.claude/scripts/<file>`) | unsupported | unsupported | unsupported | unsupported | unsupported | unsupported | unsupported | unsupported |
| steering | unsupported | native (`.kiro/steering/<name>.md`) | unsupported | unsupported | unsupported | unsupported | unsupported | unsupported | unsupported |
| hook | native (`.claude/hooks/<file>` and `.claude/settings.craftar.example.json`) | unsupported | unsupported | unsupported (through claude-code) | unsupported (through claude-code) | unsupported | converted (`.codex/hooks.json`) | converted (`.agents/hooks.json`) | unsupported |
| service | unsupported | unsupported | unsupported | unsupported | unsupported | unsupported | unsupported | unsupported | unsupported |

"through agent-skills" / "through agents-md" / "through claude-code": the tool reads that type from another target's file (for hooks, the `.claude/settings.json` that `craftar settings apply` writes); sync warns only when that target is off or the ingredient is not aimed at it, and never writes it twice.

Measured in each tool: Codex reads `.codex/agents/` only in a trusted project, and `.codex/hooks.json` only once its hooks were reviewed, an unreviewed hook is skipped silently; Antigravity run headless never applied a `glob` rule; `.github/prompts/` and `.vscode/mcp.json` are VS Code's: the Copilot CLI reads commands from `.agents/skills/` and MCP servers from `.github/mcp.json`.

`opencode` is mvp: OpenCode 2.2.5 loaded its agents, commands, skills and MCP servers through its local service, with no model; it stays mvp until a model session uses those files. It needs OpenCode 2 or later, and its rules come through `AGENTS.md`.

`service` is aimed at no AI coder: `sync` writes it under `.craftar/` for no target. `craftar targets` also prints what each converted cell changes.

## Reference (as on https://craftar.dev/docs/, Model and terms #terms, Invariants in full #guarantees)

### Model and terms

- Harness: everything that shapes how coding agents behave in a repository, rules, agents, commands, skills, hooks, MCP servers.
- Forge: one Git repository holding every ingredient, recipe and profile. Versioned; workspaces point at it by local path or by git URL, with an optional branch, tag or full SHA; a remote Forge is read from a per-machine cache. It is never a Git remote of any team repository.
- Ingredient: smallest reusable unit, a rule, agent, command, skill, hook, MCP server, script, steering file or local service. A folder with an `ingredient.yaml` declaring type, targets, inclusion mode and globs. A `service` is aimed at no AI coder: `sync` writes it under `.craftar/`. Project templates are not an ingredient: a profile declares them.
- Recipe: named set of ingredients with parameters. Recipes `extend` others; stack recipes declare a `slot` so two stacks for the same role (e.g. two front-end frameworks) cannot coexist.
- Profile: one team, its recipes, repositories, template feeds, project-management tool, internal platform, and which AI coders that team uses, and, in a Forge at `schema: 8`, its own ingredients and recipes; parameters and section overrides for the whole stack live here.
- Workspace: a local folder (one repo or a folder of repos) with a `craftar.yaml` declaring profile, recipe add/remove (edited by `craftar add recipe` / `remove recipe`) and targets, plus a git-ignored `craftar.local.yaml` for per-developer overrides.
- Target: an AI coder to emit for, eight targets working: `claude-code`, `kiro`, `agents-md`, `cursor`, `copilot`, `agent-skills` (the standard `.agents/skills/` folder), `codex` and `antigravity`; and `opencode`, mvp. Warp, Kimi and other tools read the emitted `AGENTS.md`. Coverage is a table in the CLI: `craftar targets` prints it, per ingredient type: native, converted or unsupported. Sync skips an ingredient aimed at a target that the table marks unsupported, and warns, naming it: a fallback is planned.
- Lockfile (`craftar.lock`): the Forge's source, requested ref and commit (null when the Forge is not a git repository or has no commits yet), the resolved profile, recipes and targets, and a normalized content hash for every generated file; the lock is rewritten only when its own content changes. The only authority on what Craftar owns in a workspace.
- Registry (`~/.craftar/registry.json`): every workspace a writing `sync` ran in on this machine, with path, profile, Forge, recipes, targets and last sync. `craftar workspaces` lists them with a status computed on the spot; `forget` and `prune` remove entries, and `CRAFTAR_NO_REGISTRY` turns the registry off. `craftar ui` shows them as a local page on `127.0.0.1`, read-only unless started with `--allow-writes`. `craftar ls` stays the view of one workspace's resolved recipes and ingredients.

### Invariants in full

- Never touch a file not in the lockfile: unknown files are preserved; one at a path the Forge would write is reported as a collision (FM-1).
- Never hash raw bytes: normalize LF, UTF-8, strip BOM; compare JSON structurally. Claude Code and AGENTS.md outputs keep the EOL and BOM of the file they replace; Kiro output keeps the EOL and never writes a BOM (FM-2).
- Never leave an orphan on disk: `--check` fails on it and `diff` shows it as the removal of the whole file (a hand-edited one as a header, since sync keeps it) (FM-3).
- Never require a manual mirror: everything a second target needs is generated (FM-4).
- Never split a rule from its reviewer: one ingredient, two outputs (FM-5) (planned; today the rule and its reviewer are separate ingredients (rule/<name>, agent/<name>-reviewer) grouped by a stack recipe).
- Never inline a volatile value: declared once in the profile, injected as params wherever cited (in a schema 4 Forge, inside an MCP server too; at any schema, inside a hook's `registration`, for the keys the hook declares); a parameter an ingredient declares with no default, that a file the plan writes cites and no layer sets, stops `sync`: nothing is written until it has a value (FM-6).
- Never translate: language is an attribute of the ingredient (FM-7).
- Never store a secret: an MCP ingredient declares `authEnv`, the environment variables its server needs, names only, never a value (an item shaped like a known token fails the load); with `claude-code`, `sync` writes `.claude/settings.craftar.example.json`, each declared name with an empty value; `craftar settings apply` adds a missing name, empty, to the developer's own untracked `.claude/settings.json`, and never overwrites or prints a value there; `craftar doctor` names the variables a written MCP server declares in `authEnv` or references as `${NAME}` and the environment lacks, never their values; `craftar import` refuses ingredients holding secret-like values, and a `forge:` URL holding credentials is refused; in a schema 4 Forge, a value rendered into an MCP server that is a URL with credentials or a token of a known format fails the plan, and the message names the field, never the value: a check, not a guarantee: a token of an unknown format still passes; a literal token in a hook's `registration` fails the Forge load, and a credential substituted into one fails the plan; a Forge file that is not valid YAML is reported by an error code and a position at most, never by quoting the line; one its schema refuses is reported by key, never by a value it holds (FM-8).

## Changelog (as on https://craftar.dev/changelog/, every release since 1.0.0, newest first; a summary of the README's Upgrading, or for 1.3.1, which has no section there, of its GitHub Release)

### 1.9.0: A newer Forge tag in status (2026-11-08)

- `status --json` gains `forge.newerTag`, always present and last in `forge`: the remote Forge's highest `vX.Y.Z` tag above a workspace `ref` that is itself a `vX.Y.Z` tag, else `null`. The `status` tool of `craftar mcp` and `craftar ui`'s workspace answer carry it too.
- The text of `status` gains one line when there is such a tag. No byte `sync` writes, no lock, no exit code and no network call changes: the tags come from the fetch `status` already makes, or from the cached copy.

### 1.8.0: Quieter AGENTS.md, a local recipe repointed by promote (2026-11-08)

- The `agents-md` "no AGENTS.md equivalent — skipped" warning is no longer printed for an ingredient another target of the workspace writes; it still names every ingredient no other target writes. `doctor --strict` can now exit 0 where that warning was its only `warn`.
- `craftar drift promote`: a new variant whose base a recipe in the profile's own folder cites no longer refuses: when the profile resolves that recipe, it is repointed to the variant behind the same git gate and proof.
- `opencode`: a remote MCP server whose `headers` is not an object is dropped with a warning naming the server. `craftar setup`: a new Forge's README advises keeping the Forge out of a workspace's git repository.

### 1.7.0: craftar setup, a Forge from scratch (2026-11-08)

- A new command, `craftar setup`: creates a Forge from scratch (or by importing a workspace's `.claude/`), makes it a git repository with one initial commit, and starts workspaces on it. It is the one craftar command that commits, only in the directory it creates or finds empty, and it never pushes. See https://craftar.dev/docs/#setup.
- `craftar` with no arguments, in a terminal, on a machine with no registered workspace, ends its help with `new here? run craftar setup`; the interactive `craftar init` suggests it when a Forge answer names no Forge.
- No other command changes; no byte changes for a workspace already in sync.

### 1.6.0: The opencode target, mvp (2026-11-08)

- A new target, `opencode` (OpenCode 2 or later): agents to `.opencode/agents/<name>.md` with permissions derived from their tools, commands to `.opencode/commands/<name>.md`, MCP servers to `.opencode/opencode.json`; rules reach OpenCode through `agents-md`.
- A Forge file that names `opencode` needs `schema: 18`; `craftar.lock` is written at schema 7 when it names it.
- A workspace that does not name `opencode` sees no change.

### 1.5.0: Five targets validated in each tool (2026-11-07)

- `cursor`, `copilot`, `agent-skills`, `codex` and `antigravity` were checked by opening each tool from its CLI on a synthetic workspace; the README says what was validated, per target.
- Generated bytes: `copilot` also writes `.github/mcp.json` for the Copilot CLI; `claude-code` leaves out an empty `tools` line in an agent.

### 1.4.0: A target removed (2026-11-07)

- One target is removed: the declared exception in the compatibility promise: its CLI no longer accepts Google login for individuals. Its name is refused in `targets`.
- In a workspace that used it, the files the lock recorded for it are orphans: `sync` removes them, and keeps a hand-edited one as `orphan-drift`. `antigravity` covers the same use.

### 1.3.1: Documentation only (2026-11-07)

- README and Claude Code plugin README corrections; no generated byte, lock or exit code changes.

### 1.3.0: Hooks for codex and antigravity (2026-11-07)

- Generated bytes: a hook ingredient with a `registration` is written for Codex to `.codex/hooks.json` and for Antigravity to `.agents/hooks.json`.
- `cursor` and `copilot` run the hooks `.claude/settings.json` holds, so no file of theirs is written.
- It also added a target, later removed in 1.4.0.

### 1.2.0: The codex and antigravity targets (2026-11-07)

- `codex`: agents to `.codex/agents/<name>.toml`; rules through `agents-md`, commands and skills through `agent-skills`.
- `antigravity`: rules to `.agents/rules/`, agents to `.agents/agents/`, MCP servers to `.agents/mcp_config.json`.
- A Forge file that names either needs `schema: 16`; a workspace that names neither sees no change.

### 1.1.0: The cursor, copilot and agent-skills targets (2026-11-06)

- `cursor` (`.cursor/rules/`, `.cursor/agents/`, `.cursor/mcp.json`), `copilot` (`.github/instructions/`, `.github/copilot-instructions.md`, `.github/agents/`, `.github/prompts/`, `.vscode/mcp.json`) and `agent-skills` (`.agents/skills/`).
- What a tool already reads in another target's file is not written twice.
- A Forge file that names one needs `schema: 15`; a workspace that names none sees no change.

### 1.0.0: The compatibility promise (2026-11-06)

- Nothing changes in what craftar writes. From here on, breaking a command, a flag, an exit code, a `--json` shape, the loading of a Forge schema or the reading of the lock needs a major version, and a change to generated bytes comes in a minor.

Before 1.0.0: the 0.x history, release by release, is in the README's Upgrading (https://github.com/llima/craftar-cli#upgrading) and on GitHub Releases (https://github.com/llima/craftar-cli/releases).
